name: Lactic acid + urea (Eucerin)

card.summary: Lactic acid and urea are pharmacy-aisle moisturizing and exfoliating ingredients, sold in lines such as Eucerin, that smooth rough, dry skin.
card.note: Can sting or irritate, especially on broken skin.

quick.overview:
Urea and lactic acid are two skincare ingredients found in over-the-counter moisturizers. Eucerin is a Beiersdorf brand that grew from a base ointment patented in Germany in 1902.

Urea creams are used for dry, itchy, thickened skin, and lactic acid is an alpha-hydroxy acid with exfoliating, keratolytic action. For appearance they give smoother, softer skin on the body and face.
quick.how: They are applied as creams or lotions as part of a moisturizing routine. At low concentrations urea draws moisture into the skin; at higher ones it loosens scaly buildup.
quick.risks: Side effects are generally few: mild irritation, temporary burning or stinging and itching, rarely a severe allergic reaction.

lead: Urea and lactic acid are two long-established skin-care ingredients that are often combined in pharmacy-aisle moisturizers, including products sold under the Eucerin brand. People use them on rough, dry or thickened skin, such as elbows, heels and body skin, to make it feel and look softer and smoother.[1][2]

Urea at low concentrations acts as a humectant that holds water in the outer skin, while at concentrations above about 20 percent it breaks down protein in the stratum corneum and loosens scale; preparations range from roughly 5 to 50 percent and are sold over the counter in the US.[1] Lactic acid is an alpha-hydroxy acid (AHA) with keratolytic properties, meaning it helps loosen and soften the outer skin layer, which underlies its use as a chemical exfoliant.[2][4]

Eucerin is a trademark of Beiersdorf, the Hamburg company that also makes Nivea. The brand traces to a stable ointment base created by chemist Isaac Lifschutz around 1900.[3][5] Published research on the specific Eucerin combination is not available; the evidence base consists of the separate ingredients, regulator statements on AHAs, and reviews of related lactic-acid products.

chain: Urea hydrates and loosens scale; lactic acid exfoliates
angle.text: The ingredients moisturize and exfoliate the outer skin layer, so dry or rough patches look smoother. They are used on the body and, in gentler forms, the face.

infobox: 10 percent or less, pH 3.5 or higher [6]

paras: Users apply urea and lactic-acid creams to make dry, rough or flaky skin look more even and feel softer. The chain is mechanical: urea draws and holds water in the outer layer and, at higher strengths, loosens dead scale, while lactic acid exfoliates the surface, so the dull rough layer is shed and the skin reflects light more smoothly.[1][2][4]

Alpha-hydroxy acids such as glycolic, lactic, mandelic and citric acid are used in skin care mainly for chemical exfoliation.[4] Lactic acid is also used in cosmetics to adjust a formula's acidity and has disinfectant properties.[2]

Urea cream is used for dry, itchy skin in psoriasis, dermatitis, eczema and ichthyosis, for keratosis, corns and calluses, and to soften damaged or ingrown nails. It can also help debride areas where healing is held back by infection, necrosis or eschar.[1] Wikipedia notes that urea creams have been used since the 1940s and that the World Health Organization lists them as an essential medicine.[1]

Wikipedia describes urea as working in part by loosening dried skin: it dissolves the intercellular matrix of the stratum corneum, which promotes shedding of scaly skin at higher concentrations.[1] At lower concentrations it behaves as a humectant.[1]

Lactic acid is an alpha-hydroxy acid, defined as a carboxylic acid with a hydroxyl group on the neighbouring carbon; AHAs are stronger acids than their non-alpha counterparts.[4] It is chiral, with an L form that predominates in biology, a pKa of 3.86, and it dissolves freely in water.[2]

Paul Beiersdorf founded the company in 1882 to make coated plasters, and Oscar Troplowitz bought it in 1890 and expanded it into skin care, working with dermatologist Paul Gerson Unna and chemist Isaak Lifschutz.[5] Lifschutz's emulsifier Eucerit made a stable water-and-oil cream possible, which led to Nivea Creme in 1911.[5]

Wikipedia reports that Lifschutz made a non-perishable ointment base of Eucerit, water and oil in 1900 and named it Eucerin, obtained a German patent in 1902, and that Troplowitz bought the patent in 1911.[3] The first Eucerin products, an iodine cream and a loose powder, followed in Germany a few years later; the brand was launched worldwide, including in the US, in the 1980s, and added facial care in 1996.[3] In April 2026 the UK Advertising Standards Authority banned an advert for a Eucerin face serum over a claim that users could look five years younger.[3]

Side effects of urea creams are generally few in adults: mild irritation, temporary burning, stinging and itching. Severe allergic reactions can cause rash, hives, breathing difficulty and swelling of the mouth, face, lips or tongue.[1]

For AHAs, the FDA reports that a collaborative study found topical AHA use increased sensitivity to UV light: after four weeks, sensitivity to UV-induced reddening rose 18 percent and sensitivity to UV-induced cellular damage roughly doubled on average. The effect was reversible, with no significant differences one week after stopping.[6] The Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel concluded that glycolic and lactic acid products are safe for consumers at 10 percent concentration or less, at a final pH of 3.5 or higher, and when the product protects against sun sensitivity or directs daily sun protection.[6]

The FDA received 114 adverse dermatologic reports for AHA products from 1992 to February 2004, most commonly burning, rash or dermatitis and swelling, with the most serious reactions linked to the strongest exfoliating products such as skin peelers.[6] FDA's 2005 guidance recommends a 'Sunburn Alert' statement on AHA cosmetics, with sunscreen, protective clothing and limited sun exposure during use and for a week afterwards.[6] Pure lactic acid carries corrosive hazard labelling, and the 'causes skin irritation' and 'serious eye damage' statements apply to the concentrated chemical rather than to finished creams.[2]

Cosmetic AHA products are regulated as cosmetics in the US, whereas products marketed for therapeutic purposes such as acne treatment or skin lightening are regulated as drugs.[6] Urea-containing creams are sold over the counter in the US under a range of brands including Decubal, Carmol 40 and Keralac.[1] Lactic acid is also approved as a food additive (E270) in the EU, US and Australia and New Zealand.[2]

Lactic acid is also the basis of poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA), a biodegradable polymer used as an injectable facial biostimulator such as Sculptra. This is a different compound from topical lactic acid: reviews describe PLLA microparticles stimulating collagen deposition to restore facial volume.[7] Randomised trials include a 2024 study comparing PLLA injections with no treatment for cheek wrinkles.[8]

No studies found for the combined Eucerin product. Related published work covers the ingredients separately: the FDA-collaborated UV sensitivity data and Cosmetic Ingredient Review safety conclusions for topical AHAs,[6] and clinical trials of the injectable polymer PLLA, including a 2024 randomized trial in cheek wrinkles and systematic reviews of PLLA in facial aesthetics.[7][8][9]

timeline.event: Carl Wilhelm Scheele isolates lactic acid from sour milk.[2]
Louis Pasteur identifies the role of Lactobacillus bacteria in producing lactic acid.[2]
Paul Beiersdorf founds the company in Hamburg.[5]
Isaac Lifschutz creates the Eucerin ointment base.[3]
Eucerin base ointment patented in Germany.[3]
Oscar Troplowitz buys the Eucerin patent; Nivea Creme launched.[3][5]
Eucerin launched worldwide, including the US.[3]
Eucerin begins offering facial care products.[3]
FDA guidance recommends a sunburn alert statement on AHA cosmetics.[6]
